---
title: "Working with large RAD-seq datasets"
output: html_document
date: "2026-11-10"
---



RAD-seq data assembled de novo (e.g. with
[DiscoSnpRad](https://github.com/GATB/DiscoSnp),
[Stacks](https://catchenlab.life.illinois.edu/stacks/) or
[ipyrad](https://ipyrad.readthedocs.io/)) have an unusual shape: there is no
reference genome, so each RAD locus is its own "chromosome" in the VCF (e.g.
`SNP_higher_path_1234` or `RAD_1234`), carrying one or a few SNPs. A dataset
with millions of SNPs therefore has millions of chromosomes, and every SNP
also has its own ID. Stored as strings, these names take most of the memory
of a `gen_tibble`, and much of the time needed to read, save and load it.

tidypopgen has two options to deal with this, for *VCF* files read with
`gen_tibble()` (and merged with `gt_merge_vcfs()` or `gt_concat_vcfs()`):

- `names_as_int = TRUE` stores the names of the loci as integers (the index
  of each SNP in the *VCF*);
- `chromosomes_as_int = TRUE` stores the chromosomes as integer codes. A
  chromosome whose name is a number (e.g. "7" or "chr7", or the catalog
  number of a Stacks locus) keeps that number as its code; other names (such
  as RAD loci assembled by DiscoSnpRad) are numbered in order of appearance.

Nothing is lost: the original names are written to plain text "sidecar"
files next to the backing file of the `gen_tibble`, from which
`gt_lookup_loci()`, `gt_lookup_chromosomes()` and `gt_restore_loci()` get
them back when they are needed, for example to report the hits of a scan.

In this article, we read a VCF with 18.6 million SNPs on 13.8 million RAD
loci with and without these options, compare the time and memory they need,
and then run a small analysis on the compact `gen_tibble`, looking up the
original names of the loci that come out of it.

# The data

We use a synthetic dataset with the shape of a real one: the DiscoSnpRad VCF
of the tree frog *Phyllomedusa vaillantii* (18,579,683 SNPs and 56 samples
from 3 lineages and an outgroup, 26 GB) used by
[VCFArrow](https://github.com/legalLab/VCFArrow). The full dataset is not
public, but VCFArrow ships a subsample of 10,000 SNPs and 18 samples, from
which the script `make_vcf.R`, in the
[`benchmarks/vcfarrow` folder](https://github.com/EvolEcolGroup/tidypopgen/tree/HEAD/benchmarks/vcfarrow)
of the tidypopgen repository, builds a VCF of any size with the same
features: each SNP copies the genotypes (with their missingness, about 34%)
of a random SNP of the subsample, each sample takes the genotypes of a random
sample of the same lineage, and each RAD locus (`SNP_higher_path_<n>`)
carries 1 to 5 SNPs, as in the real data.

The `bash` chunk below downloads the subsample, and runs `make_vcf.R`. This
writes the VCF, and the lineage of each of its 56 samples
(`discosnp.strata.tsv`), to `vignettes/articles/data/rad/`. NOTE: this takes
a few minutes, and needs 27 GB of disk space. As in all the chunks of this
article, the paths are relative to the folder of the article
(`vignettes/articles/` in a copy of the tidypopgen repository), which is
where R Markdown runs the chunks:


``` bash
cd ../../benchmarks/vcfarrow
mkdir -p data ../../vignettes/articles/data/rad
for f in vaillantii_discosnp_sub.vcf.gz strata; do
  curl -fsSL -o "data/$f" \
    "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/legalLab/VCFArrow/main/inst/extdata/$f"
done
Rscript make_vcf.R 18579683 ../../vignettes/articles/data/rad/discosnp.vcf 1
```

# Reading the VCF

First we load the packages, and set the path of the VCF and the number of
cores:


``` r
library(tidypopgen)
library(dplyr)
vcf_path <- "./data/rad/discosnp.vcf"
n_cores <- 4
```

We read the VCF with 4 cores, as in the VCFArrow comparison, on a machine
with 24 cores. The file is
25.3 GB.

















For RAD-seq data, we read the VCF with both options. This is the
`gen_tibble` that we use in the rest of the article:


``` r
rad_gt <- gen_tibble(vcf_path,
  backingfile = "./data/rad/rad_int",
  names_as_int = TRUE, chromosomes_as_int = TRUE,
  n_cores = n_cores, quiet = TRUE
)
```



To see what each option saves, we also read the VCF (code not shown) with the
default options, with only `names_as_int = TRUE`, and with only
`chromosomes_as_int = TRUE`, each time into a new backing file. The genotypes
are the same in all four `gen_tibble`s, and so are their backing files (the
`.bk` file, with one byte per genotype). What changes is the loci table,
which is held in memory and saved in the `.gt` file:



|options            | time_s| peak_memory_mb| loci_table_mb| bk_mb| gt_mb| sidecars_mb|
|:------------------|------:|--------------:|-------------:|-----:|-----:|-----------:|
|default            |   37.7|           3708|          2846|   924|   165|           0|
|names_as_int       |   19.9|           2552|          1756|   924|   108|         748|
|chromosomes_as_int |   19.9|           2410|          1751|   924|   125|         407|
|both               |   12.7|           1188|           660|   924|    68|        1155|



`time_s` is the time to read the VCF and save the `gen_tibble`;
`peak_memory_mb` is the largest amount of memory used by R while doing so;
`loci_table_mb` is the size of the loci table in memory; `bk_mb`, `gt_mb` and
`sidecars_mb` are the sizes of the backing file, of the `.gt` file and of the
sidecar files on disk.

With the default options, R creates a string for each of the 18.6 million
names and each of the 13.8 million chromosomes, and has to sort the
chromosomes to make the levels of a factor. With both options, the loci table
only holds integers (and the alleles, which are shared single letters), and
the names are streamed to the sidecar files while the VCF is read.

The loci table of `rad_gt` looks like this:


``` r
show_loci(rad_gt)
#> # A tibble: 17,303,683 × 7
#>    big_index  name chromosome position genetic_dist allele_ref allele_alt
#>        <int> <int>      <int>    <int>        <dbl> <chr>      <chr>     
#>  1         1     1          1       36            0 A          T         
#>  2         2     2          2       91            0 A          G         
#>  3         3     3          3       84            0 A          G         
#>  4         4     4          4       90            0 A          G         
#>  5         5     5          5       95            0 A          G         
#>  6         6     6          6       48            0 A          T         
#>  7         7     7          6       57            0 A          G         
#>  8         8     8          6       58            0 A          G         
#>  9         9     9          6       71            0 A          C         
#> 10        10    10          7       37            0 A          T         
#> # ℹ 17,303,673 more rows
```





The `.gt` file is smaller, so loading the `gen_tibble` in a new session is
faster too:


``` r
reloaded <- gt_load("./data/rad/rad_int.gt")
```



This takes 3.1 s, against
18 s for the `gen_tibble` read
with the default options (see the performance summary at the end).

# The sidecar files

The sidecars are tab separated text files next to the backing file:
`rad_int.loci.tsv` has a line for each locus, with its integer name, its
original name (the VCF ID), its chromosome and its position;
`rad_int.chromosomes.tsv` has a line for each chromosome, with its code and
its name.


``` r
cat(readLines("./data/rad/rad_int.loci.tsv", n = 4), sep = "\n")
#> int_name	name	chromosome	position
#> 1	9999998	SNP_higher_path_9999998	36
#> 2	9999997	SNP_higher_path_9999997	91
#> 3	9999994	SNP_higher_path_9999994	84
cat(readLines("./data/rad/rad_int.chromosomes.tsv", n = 4), sep = "\n")
#> int_chromosome	chromosome
#> 1	SNP_higher_path_9999998
#> 2	SNP_higher_path_9999997
#> 3	SNP_higher_path_9999994
```

They can be read with any tool and joined to
`show_loci()` by `name = int_name` (or `chromosome = int_chromosome`). Keep
them with the other files of the `gen_tibble`: `gt_get_file_names()` and
`gt_save()` list them. Functions that write a new backing file, such as
`gt_update_backingfile()`, `gt_order_loci()` and `rbind()`, write new
sidecars for it, with the loci that they keep.

# Quality control

We add the lineage of each sample, from the `strata` file of the dataset:


``` r
strata <- read.delim("./data/rad/discosnp.strata.tsv")
rad_gt <- rad_gt %>%
  mutate(population = strata$pop[match(id, strata$id)])
table(rad_gt$population)
#> 
#> BS GS OG WA 
#> 18 18  3 17
```

and remove the loci with more than 20% of missing genotypes, or with a minor
allele frequency below 5%:


``` r
loci_missing <- loci_missingness(rad_gt, n_cores = n_cores)
loci_freq <- loci_maf(rad_gt, n_cores = n_cores)
rad_gt <- rad_gt %>%
  select_loci(which(loci_missing <= 0.2 & loci_freq >= 0.05))
count_loci(rad_gt)
#> [1] 3605716
```

# A scan for differentiated loci

As a simple scan, we look for the loci whose allele frequencies differ most
between two lineages, GS and BS:


``` r
freq <- rad_gt %>%
  group_by(population) %>%
  loci_alt_freq(n_cores = n_cores, type = "matrix")
freq_diff <- abs(freq[, "GS"] - freq[, "BS"])
```

The loci table gives the integer names and chromosome codes of the hits. We
keep the frequency difference as an extra column (the synthetic data
resample the genotypes of a few samples of each lineage, so many loci have
different fixed alleles in the two lineages):


``` r
hits <- show_loci(rad_gt) %>%
  mutate(freq_diff = freq_diff) %>%
  filter(freq_diff > 0.95)
hits
#> # A tibble: 151,233 × 8
#>    big_index  name chromosome position genetic_dist allele_ref allele_alt
#>        <int> <int>      <int>    <int>        <dbl> <chr>      <chr>     
#>  1         6     6          6       48            0 A          T         
#>  2        80    80         58       88            0 A          C         
#>  3       146   146        106       45            0 A          G         
#>  4       448   448        335       32            0 A          G         
#>  5       454   454        337       97            0 A          G         
#>  6       715   715        535       68            0 T          G         
#>  7      1142  1142        876       56            0 A          T         
#>  8      1216  1216        938       90            0 C          G         
#>  9      1356  1356       1038       46            0 T          C         
#> 10      1370  1370       1050       63            0 C          T         
#> # ℹ 151,223 more rows
#> # ℹ 1 more variable: freq_diff <dbl>
```

`gt_lookup_loci()` gives back the same table, with the original names and
chromosomes. The first lookup in a session indexes the sidecar files (a
single read through each file); later lookups only read the parts of the
files that hold the loci:


``` r
hits_named <- gt_lookup_loci(rad_gt, hits)
```


``` r
hits_named
#> # A tibble: 151,233 × 8
#>    big_index name      chromosome    position genetic_dist allele_ref allele_alt
#>        <int> <chr>     <chr>            <int>        <dbl> <chr>      <chr>     
#>  1         6 9999990_1 SNP_higher_p…       48            0 A          T         
#>  2        80 9999911   SNP_higher_p…       88            0 A          C         
#>  3       146 9999834   SNP_higher_p…       45            0 A          G         
#>  4       448 9999438_1 SNP_higher_p…       32            0 A          G         
#>  5       454 9999435_1 SNP_higher_p…       97            0 A          G         
#>  6       715 9999075_5 SNP_higher_p…       68            0 T          G         
#>  7      1142 9998494   SNP_higher_p…       56            0 A          T         
#>  8      1216 9998381_2 SNP_higher_p…       90            0 C          G         
#>  9      1356 9998205_1 SNP_higher_p…       46            0 T          C         
#> 10      1370 9998180   SNP_higher_p…       63            0 C          T         
#> # ℹ 151,223 more rows
#> # ℹ 1 more variable: freq_diff <dbl>
```

`gt_lookup_loci()` also takes row numbers of the loci table, so we can look
up the top 10 hits using `order()`. Since lookups use the integer names,
rather than the rows, a table of hits stays valid if the `gen_tibble` is
filtered or reordered later.


``` r
top_10 <- gt_lookup_loci(rad_gt, order(freq_diff, decreasing = TRUE)[1:10])
```


``` r
top_10
#> # A tibble: 10 × 7
#>    big_index name      chromosome    position genetic_dist allele_ref allele_alt
#>        <int> <chr>     <chr>            <int>        <dbl> <chr>      <chr>     
#>  1         6 9999990_1 SNP_higher_p…       48            0 A          T         
#>  2        80 9999911   SNP_higher_p…       88            0 A          C

#>  5       454 9999435_1 SNP_higher_p…       97            0 A          G         
#>  6       715 9999075_5 SNP_higher_p…       68            0 T          G         
#>  7      1142 9998494   SNP_higher_p…       56            0 A          T         
#>  8      1216 9998381_2 SNP_higher_p…       90            0 C          G         
#>  9      1356 9998205_1 SNP_higher_p…       46            0 T          C         
#> 10      1370 9998180   SNP_higher_p…       63            0 C          T
```

# Summaries by RAD locus

Statistics by chromosome have one row per RAD locus, with the code of the
chromosome. For example, the number of SNPs on each RAD locus:


``` r
snps_per_locus <- show_loci(rad_gt) %>%
  count(chromosome, name = "n_snps")
table(snps_per_locus$n_snps)
#> 
#>       1       2       3       4       5 
#> 3116955  209678   21093    1474      46
```

`gt_lookup_chromosomes()` gives the names of the codes, e.g. of the RAD loci
with the most SNPs left after quality control:


``` r
top_loci <- snps_per_locus %>%
  slice_max(n_snps, n = 5, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  mutate(rad_locus = gt_lookup_chromosomes(rad_gt, chromosome))
```


``` r
top_loci
#> # A tibble: 5 × 3
#>   chromosome n_snps rad_locus              
#>        <int>  <int> <chr>                  
#> 1      93697      5 SNP_higher_path_9839771
#> 2     136215      5 SNP_higher_path_9767256
#> 3     275564      5 SNP_higher_path_9528822
#> 4     335897      5 SNP_higher_path_9425016
#> 5     915884      5 SNP_higher_path_8430712
```

# Restoring the names

When a `gen_tibble` has been filtered down to fewer loci, it can be
convenient to have the original names back in its loci table, e.g. before
exporting the data. `gt_restore_loci()` does this (it gives the same loci
table as reading the VCF with the default options, for the loci that are
kept):


``` r
rad_hits <- rad_gt %>%
  select_loci(which(freq_diff > 0.95)) %>%
  gt_restore_loci()
```


``` r
show_loci(rad_hits)
#> # A tibble: 151,233 × 7
#>    big_index name      chromosome    position genetic_dist allele_ref allele_alt
#>        <int> <chr>     <fct>            <int>        <dbl> <chr>      <chr>     
#>  1         6 9999990_1 SNP_higher_p…       48            0 A          T         
#>  2        80 9999911   SNP_higher_p…       88            0 A          C         
#>  3       146 9999834   SNP_higher_p…       45            0 A          G         
#>  4       448 9999438_1 SNP_higher_p…       32            0 A          G         
#>  5       454 9999435_1 SNP_higher_p…       97            0 A          G         
#>  6       715 9999075_5 SNP_higher_p…       68            0 T          G         
#>  7      1142 9998494   SNP_higher_p…       56            0 A          T         
#>  8      1216 9998381_2 SNP_higher_p…       90            0 C          G         
#>  9      1356 9998205_1 SNP_higher_p…       46            0 T          C         
#> 10      1370 9998180   SNP_higher_p…       63            0 C          T         
#> # ℹ 151,223 more rows
```

# Performance summary



|step                    | time_s| peak_memory_mb|
|:-----------------------|------:|--------------:|
|read_default            |  37.73|           3708|
|read_names_as_int       |  19.89|           2552|
|read_chromosomes_as_int |  19.93|           2410|
|read_both_as_int        |  12.70|           1188|
|load_default            |  18.00|           3755|
|load_both_as_int        |   3.10|           1272|
|loci_qc                 |   0.44|           1786|
|scan                    |   0.08|            811|
|lookup_first            |   0.65|            798|
|lookup_again            |   0.11|            800|
|lookup_chromosomes      |   0.02|            865|
|restore                 |   0.37|            879|



`peak_memory_mb` is the memory used by R; the genotypes are in the backing
files, on disk, and are read a block at a time by the functions that use
them.

# Key takeaways

- For RAD-seq data assembled de novo, read the *VCF* with
  `names_as_int = TRUE` and `chromosomes_as_int = TRUE`. The loci table then
  holds only integers, and reading, saving and loading the `gen_tibble` are
  faster and use much less memory.
- Nothing is lost: the original names are in the sidecar files next to the
  backing file. `gt_lookup_loci()` gives back the names of the hits of a scan
  (from a subset of the loci table, or from row numbers),
  `gt_lookup_chromosomes()` translates chromosome codes, and
  `gt_restore_loci()` puts the names back into a (smaller) `gen_tibble`.
- Keep the sidecar files with the other files of the `gen_tibble`.
- The same options are available in `gt_merge_vcfs()` and
  `gt_concat_vcfs()`, e.g. to merge several RAD-seq runs (for RAD loci
  assembled separately in each run, the loci of different runs only match if
  they have the same chromosome and position, so assemble them together).
